content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In Christian teaching, 'meat' (often rendered 'solid food' in modern translations) most commonly symbolizes advanced or mature spiritual teaching—deeper doctrine suited to spiritually grown believers—in explicit contrast to 'milk,' the elementary teaching given to spiritual infants.","primary_basis":["1 Corinthians 3:1-2 ('I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it')","Hebrews 5:12-14 ('ye are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat... strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age')","1 Peter 2:2 (the 'milk of the word' contrast, cited to frame the milk/meat progression)","1 Corinthians 2:6 (wisdom spoken 'among them that are mature,' often paired with 3:1-2)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Doing the will of God as spiritual nourishment: Jesus' statement 'My meat is to do the will of him that sent me' (John 4:32-34) makes 'meat' a symbol of obedience and mission as the believer's true sustenance.","basis":["John 4:32-34","John 6:27 ('labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Meat as a test case of Christian liberty and conscience: food sacrificed to idols and disputes over eating meat function in teaching as an emblem of freedom exercised in love toward weaker believers (less a symbol than a paradigmatic ethical issue).","basis":["Romans 14:1-23 (esp. 14:15, 14:20-21)","1 Corinthians 8:1-13 (esp. 8:13)","1 Corinthians 10:23-33"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Meat as carnal craving or fleshly appetite: Israel's lust for meat in the wilderness is read as a figure of discontent, sensual desire, and rejection of God's provision.","basis":["Numbers 11:4-34 (the quail and Kibroth-hattaavah)","Psalm 78:18-31","Psalm 106:14-15"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"'Meat in due season' as faithful pastoral teaching: the faithful servant who gives the household 'meat in due season' is read as the minister providing timely spiritual instruction.","basis":["Matthew 24:45","Luke 12:42"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The 'meat offering' (KJV term for the grain offering) as a type of Christ's sinless humanity and consecrated life, developed in typological and devotional commentary on Leviticus.","basis":["Leviticus 2:1-16","Leviticus 6:14-18"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Christ's flesh as true food ('my flesh is meat indeed'), read eucharistically or as feeding on Christ by faith, depending on tradition.","basis":["John 6:55 ('For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed')","John 6:51-58"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"An important complication is translational: in the KJV, 'meat' usually means food in general (Greek broma/trophe; Hebrew okel), not animal flesh specifically, so many 'meat' passages are simply about food. The recognizable symbolic consensus centers on the milk-versus-meat (solid food) contrast in 1 Corinthians 3 and Hebrews 5, which is a staple of sermons and commentaries on spiritual maturity. The John 6 'flesh as meat' reading is prominent but is normally discussed as eucharistic/christological doctrine rather than as symbolism of the word 'meat' per se. Prominence labels reflect how frequently each reading appears in mainstream published interpretation across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant sources."}
